A Closer Cut:
Computing Near-Optimal Lawn Mowing Tours

Sándor P. Fekete ††thanks: Department of Computer Science, TU Braunschweig, Braunschweig, Germany    Dominik Krupke11footnotemark: 1    Michael Perk11footnotemark: 1    Christian Rieck11footnotemark: 1    Christian Scheffer ††thanks: Faculty of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Bochum University of Applied Sciences, Bochum, Germany
Abstract

For a given polygonal region PP, the Lawn Mowing Problem (LMP) asks for a shortest tour TT that gets within Euclidean distance 1 of every point in PP; this is equivalent to computing a shortest tour for a unit-disk cutter CC that covers all of PP. As a geometric optimization problem of natural practical and theoretical importance, the LMP generalizes and combines several notoriously difficult problems, including minimum covering by disks, the Traveling Salesman Problem with neighborhoods (TSPN), and the ∃ℝ\exists\mathbb{R}-complete Art Gallery Problem (AGP). So far, there have only been theoretical approximation algorithms with worst-case bounds of 2​3​αTSP≈3.46​αTSP2\sqrt{3}\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize{TSP}}}\approx 3.46\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize{TSP}}}, where αTSP\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize{TSP}}} is the approximation factor for the geometric TSP. Here, αTSP=1+ε\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize{TSP}}}=1+\varepsilon is theoretically possible by using one of the famous geometric approximation schemes; however, these methods are not practically applicable for concrete instances. Moreover, there have not been any exact methods for the LMP that compute provably near-optimal solutions for instances of interesting size, owing to the combination of geometric difficulties, such as a succinct characterization of optimal solutions, as well as the lack of useful lower bounds that provide practically small performance gaps.

In this paper, we conduct the first study of the Lawn Mowing Problem with a focus on practical computation of near-optimal solutions. To this end, we provide new theoretical insights: Optimal solutions are polygonal paths with a bounded number of vertices, i.e., they do not have any curved pieces, allowing a restriction to straight-line solutions; on the other hand, there can be relatively simple instances for which optimal solutions require a large class of irrational coordinates. On the practical side, we present a primal-dual approach with provable convergence properties based on solving a special case of the TSPN restricted to witness sets. In each iteration, this establishes both a valid solution and a valid lower bound, and thereby a bound on the remaining optimality gap. As we demonstrate in an extensive computational study, this allows us to achieve provably optimal and near-optimal solutions for a large spectrum of benchmark instances with up to 20002000 vertices.

1 Introduction

There are many facets of theoretical and practical difficulty of geometric optimization problems. On the theoretical side, the classic Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) is NP-hard, making it unlikely that there is a polynomial-time algorithm that produces provably optimal solutions. Moreover, it is unknown how to efficiently evaluate a sum of square roots, so it is unclear whether the TSP for a set of points in the plane with Euclidean distances even belongs to NP. For the famous Art Gallery Problem (AGP) of finding a minimum number of guards to cover a simple polygon based on visibility, membership in NP is indeed unlikely, as it belongs to the class ∃ℝ\exists\mathbb{R}. Furthermore, problems of optimal covering are also known to be prohibitively difficult from a practical perspective: Even the largest square that can be covered by nn unit disks has only been established up to n=7n=7.

We consider a geometric optimization problem that generalizes and combines these challenges. In the Lawn Mowing Problem (LMP), we are given a (not necessarily simple or even connected) polygonal region PP and a disk cutter CC of radius rr; the task is to find a closed roundtrip of minimum Euclidean length such that the cutter “mows” all of PP, i.e., a shortest tour that moves the center of CC within distance rr from every point in PP. The LMP naturally occurs in a wide spectrum of practical applications, such as robotics, manufacturing, farming, quality control and image processing, so it is of both theoretical and practical importance.

Given that the LMP combines the Euclidean TSP, the AGP, and covering by disks, it is not surprising that it is also both theoretically and practically difficult: It is NP-hard (as it generalizes the TSP), membership in NP is unclear (as it involves evaluating Euclidean distances); it is also extremely hard from a practical perspective (as it comprises covering by disks). In fact, the only known positive algorithmic result is an approximation algorithm with a factor of 2​3​αTSP≈3.46​αTSP2\sqrt{3}\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize{TSP}}}\approx 3.46\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize{TSP}}} [7], where αTSP\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize{TSP}}} is the factor for the geometric TSP. So far, no results aiming at methods with practically good performance are known, in part because of the difficulties of (I) characterizing optimal solutions (due to the continuous nature of the LMP) and of (II) providing tight lower bounds: Neither the area of PP nor its diameter can provide such bounds, as replacing PP by a dense subset of points with zero area does not change the length of an optimal tour, which can be much longer than the diameter of PP.

1.1 Our contribution

We provide a number of theoretical and practical results for the Lawn Mowing Problem.

  • •

    We establish a characterization of optimal lawn mowing tours by proving that an optimal tour for a polygonal region PP consists of line segments between a finite set of vertices. This allows a focus on polygonal solutions, and the ensuing primal-dual scheme.

  • •

    On the other hand, we show that even relatively simple regions PP can require LMP solutions with a wide range of irrational vertices. While this does not establish ∃ℝ\exists\mathbb{R}-hardness, it gives some indication of the underlying difficulty, as it did for the AGP.

  • •

    We establish a primal-dual algorithm for the LMP by iteratively covering an expanding witness set of finitely many points in PP. In each iteration, computing a lower bound involves solving a special case of a TSP instance with neighborhoods, the Close-Enough TSP (CETSP) to provable optimality; for an upper bound, this is enhanced to provide full coverage. In each iteration, this establishes both a valid solution and a valid lower bound, and thereby a bound on the remaining optimality gap. (See Figure 1 for an illustration.)

  • •

    We prove that this discretization method leads to provably good results: both the uncovered area and the maximum distance of points from the region swept by our lower-bound tours converge to zero as we enhance the witness set.

  • •

    We present a comprehensive study to demonstrate the practical usefulness of our methods, based on a wide spectrum of benchmark instances with up to 2000 vertices. The outcomes include provably optimal solutions, limited optimality gaps, and improved lower bounds.

1.2 Related work

There is a wide range of practical applications for the LMP, including manufacturing [9, 35, 36], cleaning [17], robotic coverage [19, 20, 33, 38], inspection [27], CAD [26], farming [11, 21, 45] and pest control [13]. In Computational Geometry, the Lawn Mowing Problem was first introduced by Arkin et al. [6], who later gave the currently best approximation algorithm with a performance guarantee of 2​3​αTSP≈3.46​αTSP2\sqrt{3}\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize{TSP}}}\approx 3.46\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize{TSP}}} [7], where αTSP\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize{TSP}}} is the performance guarantee for an approximation algorithm for the TSP; while αTSP\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize{TSP}}} may be (1+ε)(1+\varepsilon) in theory, based on the methods of Arora [10] or Mitchell [42], neither approach is practically useful. A variant (in which cost was incurred both for traveling and covering) was considered by Fekete et al. [30], who gave a 4-approximation for the special case of polyominoes. Closely related is the TSP with neighborhoods (TSPN), for which it suffices to visit a neighborhood for each of a given set of discrete vertices; this was first considered by Arkin and Hassin [8], in a graph setting by Gendreau et al. [34], for “fat” neighborhoods by Mitchell [43] and heuristically by Yuan and Zhang [48]. A particularly relevant special case of the TSPN is the Close-Enough TSP (CETSP), in which it suffices to get within a Euclidean distance of rr, i.e., for which the neighborhood is an rr-disk. Dumitrescu and Tóth [24] gave an O⁡(1)O(1) approximation; they also provide a broad overview of other theoretical results for the TSPN. Practical methods were considered by Mennell [41], Behdani and Smith [14], and Coutinho et al. [22].

The Art Gallery Problem (AGP) is connected to our work by a combination of theoretical and practical issues. Also a problem of optimal geometric covering, the AGP has to deal with the theoretical difficulties of possibly irrational coordinates, as shown by Abrahamsen et al. [1] (answering an open problem by Fekete [3]); subsequently, this result served as a stepping stone towards a proof of ∃ℝ\exists\mathbb{R}-completeness [2]. On the practical side, powerful methods (e.g., by Baumgartner et al. [12], Kröller et al. [39], or de Rezende et al. [23]) for computing a good set of guards for a polygonal region PP are based on finding solutions for discrete witness sets within PP, leading to a primal-dual optimization method; see [18] for an animated multimedia description. This approach is closely related to our primal-dual method for the LMP.

Optimally covering even relatively simple regions by a set of nn unit disks has received a considerable attention, but is excruciatingly difficult. For covering rectangles by nn unit disks, Heppes and Mellissen [37] gave optimal solutions for n≤5n\leq 5; Melissen and Schuur [40] extended this for n=6,7n=6,7. See the website by Friedman [32] for illustrations of the best known solutions (only some of which are proven to be optimal) for n≤12n\leq 12. As early as 1915, Neville [44] computed the optimal arrangement for covering a disk by five unit disks, but reported a wrong optimal value; much later, Bezdek [15, 16] gave the correct value for n=5,6n=5,6. As recently as 2005, Fejes Tóth [47] established optimal values for n=8,9,10n=8,9,10. The question of incomplete coverings was raised in 2008 by Connelly; Szalkai [46] gave an optimal solution for n=3n=3. Progress on covering by (not necessarily equal) disks has been achieved by Fekete et al. [28, 29].

1.3 Preliminaries

A (simple) polygon PP is a (non-self-intersecting) shape in the plane, bounded by a finite number nn of line segments. The boundary of a polygon PP is denoted by ∂P\partial P. A tour is a closed continuous curve T:[0,1]→ℝ2T:[0,1]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2} with T⁡(0)=T⁡(1)T(0)=T(1); we denote the (Euclidean) length of TT by ℓ⁡(T)\ell(T). The cutter CC is a disk of radius rr, centered in its midpoint. The Minkowski sum of two sets A,B⊂ℝ2A,B\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} is the set A⊕B={a+b|a∈A,b∈B}A\oplus B=\{a+b\ |\ a\in A,\,b\in B\}. The coverage of a tour TT with the disk cutter CC is T⊕CT\oplus C. The coverage of a point p∈Tp\in T is {p}⊕C\{p\}\oplus C. A lawn mowing tour TT of a polygon PP with a cutter CC is a tour whose coverage contains PP. An optimal lawn mowing tour T∗T^{*} is a lawn mowing tour of shortest length. For a discrete set of points PP, a tour TT traverses PP if P⊂TP\subset T, i.e., for each p∈Pp\in P there is a t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] such that T⁡(t)=pT(t)=p.

2 Optimal tours are straight

In general, a lawn mowing tour may consist of line segments and curved arcs. We show that any optimal tour mowing a polygon can only contain line segments.

Theorem 2.1

For every polygon PP and a circular cutter, an optimal lawn mowing tour TT exclusively consists of a set of line segments.

2.1 Outline of the proof

Because our proof of Theorem 2.1 is rather technical, we formulate various lemmata within its context, see Figure 2. By means of these lemmata, the proof is partitioned as follows.

Lemma 2.1.

The key lemma for the proof of Theorem 2.1 is that given an optimal tour, the coverage of a curved arc cannot contain a region that is covered more than once.

Lemma 2.2.

Based on Lemma 2.1, we show that each point pp from the boundary of an arc tt has two closest points q,rq,r from the optimal tour.

Lemma 2.3.

We show that the two closest points q,rq,r to pp lie in a line with pp; we call rr the successor of qq.

Theorem 2.1.

Alternately applying Lemmas 2.2 and 2.3 leads to a sequence of successors on a common line, with a final successor r′r^{\prime} outside the polygon. This implies that the final successor lies on an arc that covers a region outside of the polygon, leading to a contradiction by Lemma 2.1.

2.2 Preliminaries for the proof

A (curved) arc is the image of a smooth function t:[0,1]→ℝ2t:[0,1]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2} that is either strongly convex or strongly concave, see Figure 3. A segment is the image of a linear function t:[0,1]→ℝ2t:[0,1]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2}. A component tt is an arc or a segment. We call t⁡(0)t(0) and t⁡(1)t(1) the start and end point of tt. Any tour T:[0,1]→ℝ2T:[0,1]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2} can be partitioned into a sequence of components t0,…,tk−1t_{0},\dots,t_{k-1}, such that the end point of tit_{i} equals the start point of ti+1modkt_{i+1\bmod k} for i∈{0,…,k−1}i\in\{0,\dots,k-1\}.

For any component tt, the coverage strip S⁡(t)S(t) is the region derived as the Minkowski sum C⊕tC\oplus t. The boundary ∂S⁡(t)\partial S(t) can be partitioned into four curves as follows, see Figure 3: For each point pp on the boundary, we consider its closest point N⁡(p)N(p) on tt regarding the Euclidean metric. The closure of all points pp on the boundary such that N⁡(p)N(p) is neither the start nor the endpoint of tt is the union of two way-connected components. In particular, when following the boundary of S⁡(t)S(t) in clockwise orientation, the “convex” component (denoted by S+​(t)S^{+}(t)) has positive curvature, while the “concave” component (denoted by S−​(t)S^{-}(t)) has negative curvature; see Figure 3. If it is clear from the context, we denote by S+:=S+​(t)S^{+}:=S^{+}(t), S−:=S−​(t)S^{-}:=S^{-}(t), and S:=S⁡(t)S:=S(t).

2.3 Details of the proof

A simple observation is that any tour can be partitioned into a set of line segments and curved arcs. To show that the optimality of a tour excludes the existence of a curved arc, we consider for the sake of contradiction an optimal lawn mowing tour T:={t0,…,tk−1}T:=\{t_{0},\dots,t_{k-1}\} for a circular cutter CC with at least one curved arc t:=tit:=t_{i}. Note that all our arguments are independent from the cutter’s radius.

The key lemma for the proof is that “shortcutting” curved arcs by line segments while maintaining the coverage of the entire tour reduces its length.

Lemma 2.1

Let a​bab be a segment inside of the coverage strip SS of a curved arc tt, with its end points a,ba,b on the convex side S+S^{+} of SS. Let AA be the region bounded by a​bab and S+S^{+}. If AA does not have to be covered by tt (because it is already covered otherwise), then TT is not optimal.

Let N⁡(a),N⁡(b)∈tN(a),N(b)\in t be the closest points to a,ba,b, respectively. Replacing the part of tt between N⁡(a)N(a) and N⁡(b)N(b) by the segment N⁡(a)​N​(b)N(a)N(b) results in a shorter tour, see Figure 4(a). This tour still covers the polygon, because the arc-segment-arc sequence (t1,N⁡(a)​N​(b),t2)(t_{1},N(a)N(b),t_{2}) covers SS, except for the region AA that by assumption does not have to be covered by the sequence. Thus the tour containing the original arc tt was not optimal.

 

   

 

The following corollary is straightforward.

Corollary 2.1

Let rr be a point on the tour TT, and tt be an arc of TT. If the coverage of rr intersects the convex side S+S^{+} of tt, then TT is not optimal, see Figure 4(b).

Note that in the context of Lemma 2.1 shortcutting tt by inserting the segment N⁡(a)​N​(b)N(a)N(b) is allowed, i.e., still maintains a covering tour, because the region AA does not have to be covered by tt. Simultaneously, we obtain another region A′A^{\prime} that is now additionally covered by the coverage strip of N⁡(a)​N​(b)N(a)N(b), see Figure 4(a). Intuitively speaking, A′A^{\prime} allows for another application of Lemma 2.1 to another coverage strip, and so on.

For the remaining details, denote by pp an inner point of the polygon, which lies also in the interior of the convex side S+S^{+}, i.e., a point pp whose closest point on tt is neither t⁡(0)t(0) nor t⁡(1)t(1). We show that pp needs to have two closest points on TT.

Lemma 2.2

pp has at least two closest points on TT.

As pp lies in the interior of a convex side, there is a point N⁡(p)N(p) on an arc tt and within a distance of 11 to pp. By assumption, pp does not lie on the boundary of the polygon, so there is at least a second point rr from which the cutter covers pp, as otherwise there is an uncovered region, see Figure 5(a). Assume one of these points has a smaller distance to pp, see Figure 5(b). Corollary 2.1 implies that TT is not optimal, a contradiction.          

In the context of Lemma 2.2, we call rr the successor of N⁡(p)N(p). As tt is smooth, S+S^{+} is smooth as well. Hence, the tangent to S+S^{+} in pp is well-defined. We say that a segment lies orthogonal to S+S^{+} in pp when it intersects the tangent to S+S^{+} in pp orthogonally.

Lemma 2.3

The segment between qq and its successor rr lies orthogonal to S+S^{+} in pp.

Cutter boundaries centered at qq and rr share at least the point pp. Assume that q​rqr does not intersect S+S^{+} orthogonally in pp. This implies that at least one of the cutters contains another point from the interior of S+S^{+}, because pp is an inner point of S+S^{+}, see Figure 6(a). Corollary 2.1 implies that TT is not optimal, a contradiction.          

Combining Lemmas 2.2 and 2.3 yield the following.

Corollary 2.2

pp has exactly two closest points on TT.

Intuitively, the convex side S+S^{+} of tt is squeezed between two cutters centered in qq and rr. Applying Lemmas 2.1, 2.2, and 2.3 yields a proof of Theorem 2.1, which we restate here.

See 2.1

Applying Lemmas 2.2 and 2.3 yields the existence of the successor rr of qq, such that pp, qq, and rr lie in a line that intersects S+S^{+} of tt orthogonally in pp.

To ensure that rr does not lie on a segment, we slightly perturb pp in the interior of S+S^{+}, such that rr lies on an arc. In particular, let r1r_{1} and r2r_{2} be two successors resulting from two different points p1p_{1} and p2p_{2} from the interior of S+S^{+}, such that r1r_{1} and r2r_{2} lie on segments s1s_{1} and s2s_{2}, respectively. s1s_{1} lies orthogonal to r1​p1r_{1}p_{1}; otherwise Lemma 2.1 implies that the entire tour is not optimal, see Figure 7(a). Analogously, we conclude that s2s_{2} lies orthogonal to r2​p2r_{2}p_{2}. Hence, s1s_{1} and s2s_{2} are different segments, see Figure 7(b). As the set of segments is a discrete set, there is a point pp in the interior of S+S^{+}, such that the resulting successor does not lie on a segment, as S+S^{+} is continuous. An analogous argument implies that there is a point pp in the interior of S+S^{+}, such that the successor rr is neither a point on a segment nor a start or endpoint of an arc, i.e., rr is an inner point of an arc.

This argument of the existence of a successor from the interior of an arc is repeated, resulting in a sequence R={r,…,r′}R=\{r,\dots,r^{\prime}\} of successors lying on a line. At some point in this process, a successor r′r^{\prime} is reached, fulfilling exactly one of the following cases: (1) Either the segment q​r′qr^{\prime} crosses the boundary of the polygon (see Figure 8(a)), or (2) the convex side of the arc of r′r^{\prime} touches the polygon boundary in a point ss (see Figure 8(b)). This means that the line q​r′qr^{\prime} lies orthogonal to the boundary of PP. In this situation, we denote the intersection point of q​r′qr^{\prime} with the coverage of r′r^{\prime} by ss, which is equal to the intersection between q​r′qr^{\prime} and ∂P\partial P.

In the first case, we obtain a region AA that must not be covered by the tour, hence Lemma 2.1 implies that TT cannot be optimal.

In the second case, we perturb pp including the entire constructed sequence RR of successors and the intersection point ss of the ray p​r′pr^{\prime} with ∂P\partial P. This results in the scenario that ss is an inner point of PP, leading to a continuation of the construction of successors until the first case is reached. This concludes the proof.          

3 Irrational tour vertices

In the previous section we saw that optimal lawn mowing tours must be polygonal paths. This makes it critical to characterize coordinates of potential tour vertices. As we show in the following, irrational coordinates may be involved in an optimal tour, indicating possible algebraic (and hence algorithmic) difficulties.

Theorem 3.1

For any rational number 0<λ≤20<\lambda\leq 2, there are simple polygons PP with rational vertex coordinates for which an optimal lawn mowing tour contains a vertex with a coordinate of h:=1−(λ/2)2h:=\sqrt{1-{\left(\lambda/2\right)}^{2}}.

For 0<λ≤20<\lambda\leq 2, let P=(a,b,c)P=(a,b,c) be the polygon with a=(0,0)a=(0,0), b=(λ,0)b=(\lambda,0), and c=(λ2,2)c=\left(\frac{\lambda}{2},2\right), see Figure 9. It is easy to see that any lawn mowing tour must have at least one point that touches the unit circles Ca,CbC_{a},C_{b}, and CcC_{c} that are centered at the vertices of PP.

We show that the point pp on the intersection of CaC_{a} and CbC_{b} within PP has to be part of the optimal lawn mowing tour, see Figure 9(a).

Assume that TT is an optimal tour, and let qq be some point on TT with q∈∂Ccq\in\partial C_{c}. For the sake of contradiction, assume that p∉Tp\not\in T. Thus, there exist two points pℓ,pr∈Tp_{\ell},p_{r}\in T, with pℓ∈∂Cap_{\ell}\in\partial C_{a}, and pr∈∂Cbp_{r}\in\partial C_{b}, see Figure 9(b). As TT connects pℓ,prp_{\ell},p_{r}, and qq, the length of the tour is ℓ⁡(T)≥d⁡(pℓ,pr)+d⁡(pℓ,q)+d⁡(pr,q)\ell(T)\geq d(p_{\ell},p_{r})+d(p_{\ell},q)+d(p_{r},q). Independent of the choice of the points pℓ,prp_{\ell},p_{r}, and qq, we observe that d⁡(pℓ,q)+d⁡(pr,q)>2​d​(p,q)d(p_{\ell},q)+d(p_{r},q)>2d(p,q). Moreover, T′=p​q​pT^{\prime}=pqp is a feasible tour with length ℓ⁡(T′)<ℓ⁡(T)\ell(T^{\prime})<\ell(T), contradicting the assumption that TT is an optimal tour.

It remains to show that pp has an irrational coordinate, and that T′T^{\prime} is the unique optimal tour. The three points a,ba,b, and pp describe an isosceles triangle of base length λ\lambda, thus the yy-coordinate of pp is 1−(λ/2)2\sqrt{1-{\left(\lambda/2\right)}^{2}}. The point qq that is closest to pp clearly lies on the vertical line x=λ2x=\frac{\lambda}{2}. It is easy to see that the tour that connects the points p=(λ2,1−(λ/2)2)p=\left(\frac{\lambda}{2},\sqrt{1-{\left(\lambda/2\right)}^{2}}\right) and q=(λ2,1)q=\left(\frac{\lambda}{2},1\right) covers PP and has length ℓ⁡(T′)=2​(1−1−(λ/2)2)\ell(T^{\prime})=2\left(1-\sqrt{1-{\left(\lambda/2\right)}^{2}}\right). Because pp has to be a vertex of the tour, and any other choice of qq results in a longer tour, T′T^{\prime} is the unique optimal lawn mowing tour for PP.          

As a consequence, bounded accuracy in computing coordinates may become an issue, motivating the concept of ε\varepsilon-robust coverage, for which any point must be covered by a portion of the cutter CC that is at least ε\varepsilon-interior to CC, corresponding to a CETSP solution with neighborhood size r−εr-\varepsilon. Furthermore, the algebraic difficulty motivates the following.

Problem 1

Is the LMP ∃ℝ\exists\mathbb{R}-complete?

4 A primal-dual approach to Lawn Mowing

Now we describe our primal-dual approach to computing good tours for the LMP, based on (i) iteratively selecting finite subsets WW of points from the uncovered portion of PP, (ii) covering WW by an optimal solution TWT_{W} for the Close-Enough TSP for WW to obtain a lower bound, (iii) enhancing TWT_{W} to a feasible covering tour of PP to obtain an upper bound.

In the following, we describe basic mechanisms and analytical implications; further technical details that affect the practical performance are described in the following Section 5.

4.1 Witness sets and Close-Enough TSP

At each stage of our algorithm, we use a finite set WW of witnesses, in PP. It is straightforward to see that these induce lower bounds on the length of an optimal lawn mowing tour.

Theorem 4.1

For W1⊂W2⊂PW_{1}\subset W_{2}\subset P, let TW1T_{W_{1}}, TW2T_{W_{2}}, and TPT_{P} be optimal lawn mowing tours for W1W_{1}, W2W_{2}, and PP, respectively. Then ℓ⁡(TW1)≤ℓ⁡(TW2)≤ℓ⁡(TP)\ell(T_{W_{1}})\leq\ell(T_{W_{2}})\leq\ell(T_{P}).

Because all points w∈Ww\in W are covered by a cutter CC of radius rr if and only if the center of CC visits all disks of radius rr centered at ww, such a Close-Enough TSP tour for WW corresponds to a lawn mowing tour for WW, and thus a lower bound for the LMP on PP. Therefore, a sequence of enhanced witness sets leads to an increasing sequence of lower bounds for ℓ⁡(TP)\ell(T_{P}); if some T⁡(Wi)T(W_{i}) is a feasible LMP tour for PP, it is optimal.

Arkin et al. [6, 7] noted that any LMP tour may need a pseudopolynomial (but not polynomially bounded) number of tour vertices even for a square-shaped lawn with diameter dd and d>>rd>>r. For ε\varepsilon-robust coverage (as defined in Section 3), we can establish a finite upper bound on the number of necessary witnesses that is independent of nn, and holds even for general sets P⊂ℝ2P\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}, not necessarily just polygons or connected sets.

Theorem 4.2

Consider a region P⊂ℝ2P\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} of diameter dd, a circular cutter CC of radius rr and some 0<ε≤r20<\varepsilon\leq\frac{r}{2}. Then there is a witness set WW of size bounded by |W|≤⌈2​d2ε2⌉∈O⁡(d2)|W|\leq\left\lceil\frac{2d^{2}}{\varepsilon^{2}}\right\rceil\in O(d^{2}), for which any ε\varepsilon-robust CETSP tour is also feasible for the LMP.

A bounding box BB of PP has dimensions at most d×dd\times d, so we can subdivide BB by an orthogonal mesh of width ε/2\varepsilon/\sqrt{2}, consisting of not more than ⌈2​d2ε2⌉\left\lceil\frac{2d^{2}}{\varepsilon^{2}}\right\rceil grid cells, Ci​jC_{ij}, each of diameter at most ε\varepsilon. Whenever P∩Ci​j≠∅P\cap C_{ij}\neq\emptyset, picking an arbitrary witness point from P∩Ci​jP\cap C_{ij} ensures that each such cell (and hence, all of PP) is covered by any ϵ\epsilon-robust CESTP tour.          

For general (and not just robust) witness sets, it is easy to see that all extreme points of PP must be contained; if PP is a convex polygon, this includes all nn vertices. Thus, no such upper bound exists in terms of only dd and rr. For other types of regions PP (such as disks), no finite bound of any kind exists, as the whole perimeter needs to be contained in a witness set.

Problem 2

For a polygon PP with nn vertices and diameter dd, and a circular cutter of radius rr, is there a witness set WW of size polynomial in nn, dd, 1/r1/r, such that an optimal CETSP solution for WW is a feasible lawn mowing tour of PP?

4.2 Lower bounds: convergence

As we enhance the witness set, we can ensure that the maximum distance of uncovered points from an ensuing CETSP tour converges to zero. This can be achieved by a relatively dense set of witness points (as in Theorem 4.2) or (more economically) by iteratively reducing this maximum distance when necessary. We get the following straightforward implication.

Lemma 4.1

Let W⊂PW\subset P be a finite set of witness points, such that no point of PP has a distance larger than δ\delta from a witness point, and let TWT_{W} be a feasible CETSP tour of WW. Then

dmax:=maxp∈P⁡minq∈TW⊕C⁡d⁡(p,q)≤δ.d_{\max}:=\max_{p\in P}\min_{q\in T_{W}\oplus C}d(p,q)\leq\delta.

In the remainder of this subsection, we will repeatedly apply the following theorem.

Theorem 4.3 (Fekete and Pulleyblank [31])

Let EE be a connected planar arrangement of edges and CC be a disk of radius rr. If LL is the total length of the edges in EE, there is a closed roundtrip of length at most 2​L+2​π​r2L+2\pi r that visits all points of the boundary of E⊕CE\oplus C.

In the sequel, EE will be the edges of a tour, leading to the following.

Theorem 4.4

Let WW be a witness set, and let TWT_{W} be an optimal CETSP tour of WW. Let the distance between uncovered points and covered region be bounded by the cutter radius rr, i.e., dmax:=maxp∈P⁡minq∈TW⊕C⁡d⁡(p,q)≤rd_{\max}:=\max_{p\in P}\min_{q\in T_{W}\oplus C}d(p,q)\leq r. Then PP has a lawn mowing tour of length at most 3​ℓ​(TW)+2​π​r+2​r3\ell(T_{W})+2\pi r+2r.

By assumption, any uncovered point p∈Pp\in P is within distance rr from the boundary of E⊕CE\oplus C. Therefore, all points that are not covered by TWT_{W} will be covered by a tour of the boundary of E⊕CE\oplus C; by Theorem 4.3, there is such a tour of length at most 2​ℓ​(TW)+2​π​r2\ell(T_{W})+2\pi r. Concatenating this tour with TWT_{W} (at additional cost at most 2​r2r) achieves full coverage of PP at cost at most 3​ℓ​(TW)+2​π​r+2​r3\ell(T_{W})+2\pi r+2r, as claimed.          

Furthermore, we can conclude the following.

Lemma 4.2

Let W0⊂W1⊂…⊂Wi⊂…⊂PW_{0}\subset W_{1}\subset\ldots\subset W_{i}\subset\ldots\subset P be a sequence of witness sets, with TWiT_{W_{i}} being the corresponding sequence of optimal CETSP tours of WiW_{i}. If the maximum distance dmax(i):=maxp∈P⁡minq∈TWi⊕C⁡d⁡(p,q)d_{\max}^{(i)}:=\max_{p\in P}\min_{q\in T_{W_{i}}\oplus C}d(p,q) of uncovered points to the covered region converges to zero, then the area of P∖TWi⊕CP\setminus T_{W_{i}}\oplus C converges to zero.

By assumption, the sequence dmax(i)d_{\max}^{(i)} converges to zero, so there is an index kk such that dmax(i)≤rd_{\max}^{(i)}\leq r for all i≥ki\geq k. Then by Theorem 4.1, all elements of the sequence ℓ⁡(TWi)\ell(T_{W_{i}}) are lower bounds of any feasible LMP tour, so by Theorem 4.4, they satisfy ℓ⁡(TWi)≤3​ℓ​(TWk)+2​π​r+2​r\ell(T_{W_{i}})\leq 3\ell(T_{W_{k}})+2\pi r+2r, i.e., remain bounded from above. Furthermore, all points in the set P∖TWi⊕CP\setminus T_{W_{i}}\oplus C of uncovered points by TWiT_{W_{i}} are within distance dmax(i)d_{\max}^{(i)} of the boundary of TWi⊕CT_{W_{i}}\oplus C; by Theorem 4.3, this boundary has length of at most L=2​ℓ​(TWi)+2​π​rL=2\ell(T_{W_{i}})+2\pi r. Moreover, the area of all points within a distance dmax(i)d_{\max}^{(i)} of any curve of length LL is bounded by Ai:=(2​L+2​π)​dmax(i)A_{i}:=(2L+2\pi)d_{\max}^{(i)}, so the total uncovered area is bounded by Ai≤(4​ℓ​(TWi)+4​π​r+2​π)​dmax(i)≤(12​ℓ​(TWk)+12​π​r+8​r+2​π)​dmax(i)A_{i}\leq(4\ell(T_{W_{i}})+4\pi r+2\pi)d_{\max}^{(i)}\leq(12\ell(T_{W_{k}})+12\pi r+8r+2\pi)d_{\max}^{(i)}. Because (12​ℓ​(TWk)+12​π​r+8​r+2​π)(12\ell(T_{W_{k}})+12\pi r+8r+2\pi) is constant and dmax(i)d_{\max}^{(i)} by assumption converges to zero, we conclude that AiA_{i} also converges to zero, implying the claim.          

We summarize.

Theorem 4.5

By picking an appropriate sequence of witness sets WiW_{i}, we can guarantee that for the ensuing sequence of optimal CETSP solutions T⁡(Wi)T(W_{i}), the following holds.

  • •

    The maximum distance of uncovered points to the covered region converges to zero.

  • •

    The total uncovered area converges to zero.

4.3 Solving CETSP instances

Solving CETSP instances is more challenging than solving TSP instances. In 2016, Coutinho et al. [22] proposed an algorithm based on branch-and-bound and Second-Order Cone Programming. Each branch-and-bound node is associated with a partial tour that visits the given subset of vertices in particular order. At the root node, the algorithm chooses three vertices to generate an initial sequence. The problem of computing the exact coordinates from a predefined sequence can be formulated as a Second-Order Cone Problem (SOCP). If the solution at the root node is feasible, the solution is optimal and the algorithm terminates. Otherwise, the algorithm branches into three subproblems, one for every edge in the current solution. At each edge a currently uncovered vertex is inserted. A node is pruned if the cost is at least equal to the best known upper bound or if its associated solution is feasible.

(4.1) minimize ∑k=1qzk\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{q}z_{k}

subject to

(4.2) xik−1−xik=wk\displaystyle x_{i_{k-1}}-x_{i_{k}}=w_{k} k=0,…,q\displaystyle k=0,\dots,q
(4.3) yik−1−yik=uk\displaystyle y_{i_{k-1}}-y_{i_{k}}=u_{k} k=0,…,q\displaystyle k=0,\dots,q
(4.4) xk¯−xk=sk\displaystyle\bar{x_{k}}-x_{k}=s_{k} k=0,…,q\displaystyle k=0,\dots,q
(4.5) yk¯−yk=tk\displaystyle\bar{y_{k}}-y_{k}=t_{k} k=0,…,q\displaystyle k=0,\dots,q
(4.6) wk2+uk2≤zk2\displaystyle w_{k}^{2}+u_{k}^{2}\leq z_{k}^{2} k=0,…,q\displaystyle k=0,\dots,q
(4.7) sk2+tk2≤rk2\displaystyle s_{k}^{2}+t_{k}^{2}\leq r_{k}^{2} k=0,…,q\displaystyle k=0,\dots,q
zk≥0;xk,yk,wk,uk,sk,tk​free\displaystyle z_{k}\geq 0;\hskip 2.84526ptx_{k},y_{k},w_{k},u_{k},s_{k},t_{k}\hskip 2.84526pt\text{free} k=0,…,q\displaystyle k=0,\dots,q

The formulation by Coutinho et al. [22] is based on work of Mennell [41]. Let S={i0,…,iq},q<nS=\{i_{0},\dots,i_{q}\},\,q<n be a partial sequence of vertices during the execution of the branch-and-bound algorithm. The desired solution must provide exact values for the coordinates (xik,yik),k=0,…,q(x_{i_{k}},y_{i_{k}}),\,k=0,\dots,q such that the length of the partial tour is minimized. Denoting i−1=iqi_{-1}=i_{q}, the formulation is as follows.

The SOCP uses variables zkz_{k} to represent the distance between subsequent vertices ik−1i_{k-1} and iki_{k} in the given sequence SS. To compute the distance, four auxiliary variables wk,uk,stw_{k},u_{k},s_{t}, and tkt_{k} are introduced in Constraints (4.2)–(4.5) that represent differences of coordinates that are used to calculate Euclidean distances. Constraints (4.6) define the length of the edge connecting subsequent vertices. Constraints (4.7) ensure that the hitting points will lie within their respective circles around viv_{i}. Andersen et al. [5] showed that a SOCP can be solved in polynomial time. The branch-and-bound approach of Coutinho et al. [22] makes use of well-known optimization software that is also capable of addressing this class of problems.

4.4 Upper bounds: obtaining feasible solutions

Given is a polygon PP, a circular cutter CC and a maximum number of iterations. We start by initializing the witness set W0W_{0} with some points p∈Pp\in P.

In each iteration ii, we start with generating a CETSP start tour TiT_{i} from WiW_{i}; see Figure 15 for families of examples. If TiT_{i} is a feasible LMP tour, it is optimal; otherwise, we can extract the uncovered regions from P∖(Ti⊕C)P\setminus(T_{i}\oplus C).

As shown in Figure 15 for each of the lower bounds, we then execute the following procedure to modify TiT_{i} until the tour becomes feasible. For every uncovered region RjR_{j}, we construct a witness set WRjW_{R_{j}} and fix the closest point pj∈∂Tip_{j}\in\partial T_{i} to RjR_{j} to be visited by a tour TiT_{i} computed by the CETSP solver.

After the tour TiT_{i} is computed, we add WRjW_{R_{j}} to obtain Wi+1W_{i+1}, so that the next start tour covers the points in WRjW_{R_{j}} from the beginning. (See Section 5.1 and again Figure 15 for practical strategies for choosing WRjW_{R_{j}}.) Subsequently, we extend TiT_{i} with TRjT_{R_{j}}, by connecting both tours via the point pjp_{j}. Once we obtain a feasible tour TiT_{i} (such as in the examples of Figure 15), we can update the best known solution so far and continue with the next iteration for lower and upper bounds, see Algorithm 1.

5 Experiments and evaluations

Now we describe our practical implementation and various algorithm engineering aspects, along with our experimental study for demonstrating the practical usefulness of our theoretical concept. All experiments were carried out on a regular desktop workstation with an AMD Ryzen 7 5800X (8×3.8 GHz8\times$3.8\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz}$) CPU and 128 GB128\text{\,}\mathrm{GB} of RAM. The code and data are publicly available11 1 Source code and data: https://github.com/tubs-alg/near-optimal-lawn-mowing-tours. Consider Figure 15 for practical illustrations of the progression of lower bounds for different witness strategies, and for the corresponding upper bounds. For carrying out our experiments and evaluations, we used the FPG, SRPG ISO and SRPF OCTA instances from the Salzburg Database of Geometric Inputs [25]. See Figure 10 for the overall distribution, and Figure 16 for a sample of individual instances. We considered polygons with up to n=2000n=2000 vertices, in combination with cutters of varying size. Overall, this resulted in several hundred instances. As it turned out, the parameter relative area, i.e., the ratio between the areas of the convex hull of PP and the cutter CC, was more significant for the difficulty of an instance than the vertex number nn, which is why we mostly focused on the variance in relative area.

5.1 Generating witness sets

As we established in the previous section, enhancing the witness set leads to convergence of the resulting lower bound tours, at least in terms of covered area and distance to uncovered points. In a practical setting, solving the involved CETSP instances becomes a bottleneck, so it becomes crucial to achieve good lower bounds with witness sets of limited size.

For the initial witness set W0W_{0}, we focus on the exterior of the polygon, as minimizing the length in further iterations will automatically pull the CETSP tour towards the interior; so we choose up to 1515 witnesses either from the convex hull, or the boundary of PP. If there are more than 1515 candidate points, we apply a greedy max-min-dispersion to achieve a well-distributed witness set. This may already lead to optimal solutions for small instances.

For further iterations, we insert 1010 more witnesses into regions that are not yet covered. For multiple uncovered regions, we do a random assignment, according to region size. Within each uncovered region RjR_{j}, we select the assigned number of new witnesses either (i) randomly, (ii) from a grid, or (iii) from the straight skeleton [4]. To avoid strongly clustered sets (which are bound to occur for the straight skeleton), we employ a dispersion technique. To prevent new witnesses from being close to the boundary but deep inside of the uncovered regions, we cluster the candidate points using kk-means, and select a random witness from each cluster.

The two strategies for choosing the initial witness set and the three strategies for extending it result in six general strategies, some of which are shown in the first three columns of Figure 15.

5.2 Practical quality of lower bounds

In each iteration, our algorithm computes an optimal CETSP tour on the current witness set; this results in an increasing sequence of lower bounds (due to Theorem 4.1), which are asymptotically tight, at least in terms of covered area and distance to uncovered points. Thus, computing exact CETSP solutions becomes critical. While we could still solve clustered instances with up to 10001000 points to optimality, they do not necessarily yield good lower bounds for the LMP; on the other hand, well-distributed witness sets much beyond 50 points were harder to solve optimally, but still yielded better bounds, illustrating the delicate balance between the structure of witness sets, CETSP solvability, and quality of lower bounds.

In the following, we use the best lower bound obtained within 55 iterations. The calls to the CETSP solver are limited to 30 min30\text{\,}\mathrm{min}, after which the best lower bound is returned. Figure 11 shows the progress of lower bound and coverage. With each iteration, the CETSP gets harder to solve, and the improvements on lower bound and coverage decrease. As shown in Figure 12 (left), the resulting lower bound after the final iteration is notably better than the lower bound derived from the diameter or area of the polygon. This is true for all three classes of instances, up to a relative area of about 5050, after which the CETSP strategy gets bogged down by too many witnesses. The lower bounds of the individual witness strategies are surprisingly close, as shown in Figure 12 (right). Starting with the convex hull gives a small advantage; otherwise, the best strategies vary strongly for the instances. Example runs of some strategies over 5 iterations are shown in Figure 15. The best way to improve these (and other) lower bounds would be to add further iterations, at the expense of runtime.

5.3 Practical quality of upper bounds

For small instances, the CETSP procedure frequently returns feasible (and hence, optimal) LMP tours. Otherwise, we perform up to 55 iterations in which we add 4040 witnesses into each uncovered area and connect the tour to the previous tour, as described in Section 4.4. For medium-sized instances, this strategy often leads to feasible solutions that are significantly better than the approximation algorithm; see Figures 13(a), 13(b), and 13(c) for an example. For instances up to a relative area of around 66, we often obtain optimal solutions, or solutions with a negligibly small gap. For instances up to a relative area of around 3030, we are at most 50 %50\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} above the lower bound, and only slightly worse for 4040. For larger instance sizes, Theorem 4.4 still bounds the relative gap to 200 %200\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}, but the CETSP computation becomes a bottleneck. For instances up to a relative area of 4040, the approximation algorithm turns out to be relatively stable at 100 %100\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} above the lower bound, which is considerable better than the classical worst-case approximation guarantee by Arkin et al. [7], which is at 2​3+ε≈3.462\sqrt{3}+\varepsilon\approx 3.46 even when disregarding some finer technical aspects: That method is based on combining a proximity approximation for considering region boundary and interior (incurring an asmyptotic factor of 3), a grid conversion (incurring a factor of 2/32/\sqrt{3}), and a TSP approximation (incurring a theoretical factor of 1+ε1+\varepsilon when using a geometric PTAS, and a larger factor when using a more practical approximation method); this results in an overall factor no better than 2​3+ε≈3.462\sqrt{3}+\varepsilon\approx 3.46, and even more when accounting for a non-asymptotic approximation factor with an additive term (see [7]) and PTAS limitations. For our experiments, however, the TSP instances in the approximation algorithm were solved to optimality.

6 Conclusion

The Lawn Mowing Problem generalizes a number of notoriously difficult geometric optimization problems, making it both important and highly challenging. We have provided progress on several aspects of the LMP, both on the theoretical and the practical side, demonstrating (for the first time ever) that practically useful progress may be achievable.

A spectrum of open problems remain. On the theoretical side, we already stated Problem 1 and Problem 2. On the practical side, two critical questions are the development of additional approaches for speeding up the computation of lower bounds, as well as more efficient ways to compute upper bounds, along with additional local improvement heuristics. In addition, the concept of ε\varepsilon-robustness deserves further exploration.
